The target line is expressed as percent of the attendance goal at fixed calendar offsets (2 weeks, 1 week), not as percent of ticket sales at marketing moments.
The signup-to-attendance drop-off is stated as the 30-50% range, not as a single figure.
100% of the attendance goal (about 600 signups) is targeted two weeks before the event.

The one-week registration close is flagged as hackathon-specific rather than generalized into a conference rule.
The position is computed as roughly 27% of expected sales and compared against the one-month checkpoint.
40-50% of expected sales at one month out is named as the on-track band.
27% is placed in the 25-30% band characteristic of a team that skipped or delayed its visibility push - an execution shortfall, not a demand verdict.
It checks whether the 380 figure is net of comps (sponsor, speaker, organizer, volunteer tickets) before trusting the percentage.
It checks whether program or speaker announcements ran later than planned.
It checks whether the theme is narrow enough to exclude part of the intended audience.
It checks whether the messaging ever actually said who is welcome, named as a funnel problem rather than a vague promote-more diagnosis.
Healthy reach and healthy conversion is named as a genuine demand read belonging to the demand-fit diagnosis and the event's own scope-downgrade decision, not to a bigger campaign.
The 40% price cut and track cancellation are not endorsed as a first response before the diagnosis.

Barter-only plus a fixed test budget is recommended as the default posture.
No cash is allocated to partner swaps, because that channel trades in reciprocal visibility rather than money.
The fixed test is one capped amount, on one paid channel, answering one question decided in advance.
The bulk of the money is held behind a decision point (released against a checkpoint), not committed in week one.
A concentrated bet is gated on a checkpoint miss combined with an existing tracked referral signal; a miss alone is named as a reason to diagnose, not to spend.
Owned channels (mailing list, comms hub, social) are costed in organizer hours, not cash.
The plan states it assumes the community-run pole before allocating anything.

Outreach extends beyond the home campus, applying the rule of inviting at least 3 schools within 6 hours, without overlooking community colleges.
A comms hub (one page centralizing every channel, shareable by QR code) is included as a one-time build that converts reach rather than creating it.
School contacts and local business or professional networks are tracked as two separate referrer pools, not one undifferentiated local list.
The ranking is presented as a default re-ranked for this organizer's context, not as a fixed law.
The response refuses to extend or move the May 30 early-bird date inside the marketing plan.
It explains the cutoff is owned by the pricing decision: moving it changes the price ladder and revenue, and the pricing checkpoint no longer measures what it did.
The campaign is planned around May 30 as a fixed date, with the reminder push timed before it.
The response declines to draft the reminder email copy itself.
Email execution is routed to the sibling that writes attendee email sequences, handing over weight, phase and send dates.
The response declines to build the two weeks of LinkedIn posts or a social content calendar.
Social execution is routed to the sibling that owns the event's social presence, with its weight, phase and dates handed over.
The early-bird close is identified as a sales-spike moment carrying the roughly-15% checkpoint on the ladder.
The slipped speaker announcement is flagged as a communication cause to check when reading the next checkpoint, since late announcements are an execution risk.
The launch spike is read as measuring reach, not demand.
Week two is identified as when the campaign pattern becomes readable.
Per-channel tracked links or registration codes are named as something decided before launch that cannot be added retroactively, which is why the existing 66 registrations are unattributable.
The 'how did you hear about us' field is flagged as undercounting owned channels and double-counting whatever the registrant saw last.
Progress is measured against the chosen spine's checkpoint line, not against day-over-day counts.
What each tracked signal would trigger is written down before the pushes launch; a miss alone triggers diagnosis, not spend.
The spine is picked by the failure that would actually hurt this event - empty seats versus unsold seats - reasoning from the nominal fee and the hard capacity cap.
Exactly one spine is run as the plan's only target line.
The other spine's checkpoint is used only as a secondary sanity check that never enters a target or a go/no-go decision.
The two denominators are named as different things: an attendance goal versus expected sales net of comps.
A halfway miss is answered with diagnosis (reach versus conversion signals) and re-weighting of owned and barter channels, not with spending.
That segment is named as one other channels never reach.
Last year's own week-by-week curve is overlaid as the primary target line, with the published checkpoint ladder as the fallback, because an event's own prior curve beats any published ladder.
The pace index is defined as tickets-to-date divided by curve-expected, times 100.
Above 100 is read as running hot and below 100 as a gap with a size and a deadline attached.
Email frequency is kept limited and the content informative, to maintain list engagement.

The plan records for the next edition: the spine chosen, the net-of-comps target, channel weights with their segments, the fixed dates, the budget posture, and planned-versus-actual at each checkpoint.
